idiom_name: closure thunks with `while (typeof step === 'function') step = step()`
implementation_notes: V8 never shipped the ES2015 proper-tail-call semantics and tc39 replaced them with a syntactic-tail-calls proposal, so the trampoline is hand-written: every mutually recursive function returns either the value or a zero-argument closure, and one loop keeps calling the closure until a non-function appears. The one-line driver is portable to every engine and needs no build step. The generator variant below keeps the same driver idea but lets the steps be pulled instead of pushed. Keep ordinary recursion while depth is bounded: the trampoline trades readable engine stack traces for one closure allocation per step.
pitfalls: A step payload that is itself a function is indistinguishable from a thunk, so the driver contract rests on a convention; use a tagged step object when the payload can be callable.
Each step allocates a closure capturing its arguments; deep walks in hot browser paths should measure the allocation against the recursion they replaced.
The engine stack can still blow in the driver's own helpers: any recursive call made outside the trampoline (logging, serialisation) is back on the JS stack.

variants.name: Generator steps pulled by an explicit driver stack
variants.idiom_name: function* steps with an iterative driver stack (next/push/pop) instead of yield*
variants.implementation_notes: Generator functions let a step hand its next step to the driver with yield, and the driver keeps an explicit stack of generators, pushing the yielded generator and popping it when it finishes (ES2015 floor). This keeps the engine stack flat and makes suspension points visible in the algorithm, which is how effect-style libraries drive long workflows. It must not use yield*, because delegation happens inside the engine and nests frames again the moment a chain is deep - the explicit driver stack is the point of the variant.
pitfalls: yield* delegates inside the engine and grows the JS stack for deep chains; the driver must own the stack explicitly.
Values and generator objects are both objects at runtime, so the driver must distinguish 'this is the next step' from 'this is a yielded value' with a marker instead of guessing.
Generators are lazily started: forgetting the first next() call leaves the step unexecuted, and mixing manual next() calls with the driver corrupts the chain.
